TELEPHONE SYSTEMS
OBJECTIVES

w Describe local area telephone calling.
EQUIPMENT REQUIRED
The telephone system used in the United States, and almost throughout the world, has developed over the last hundred years.
INTRODUCTIONM
The telephone system basically operates the same today as it did then, with two exceptions.
One, modern electronic circuits and switching devices have replaced older circuits and manual switching devices.
Two, the number of users has drastically increased. There are estimated to be over 750 million telephones in use globally, probably many more.
These two exceptions have forced the development of a standardized telephone system that can easily connect your phone to any of 500 million phones around the globe.
Let's begin the lesson on TELEPHONE SYSTEMS...............................
LESSON MENU
LOCAL AREA PHONE NETWORKWORK

You probably use the telephone set, called a TELSET for short, every day. Do you ever wonder how the telephone connects to and rings a friend's phone, why some calls are considered long distance, and how does the telephone connect overseas?
DISCUSSION
The telset is just one small part of a complete system that must be able to connect any telset to another telset.
Basically, there are three methods that can be used to connect telsets: direct connection, switching, and hierarchy. Only one method is practical when considering the number of telsets in use today.
The direct connection method means that each telset is directly connected. The example below shows six telsets directly connected.

This method is the simplest but, not very practical today. Each telset is connected to another using two wires per connection. If you were connecting 500 million telsets to yours, you would have 1 billion wires running into your house, not very practical.
Using the switching method telsets are connected through one station.
This method was developed as more and more telsets were used.
However, one switching station for 500 million telsets is still impractical.
The hierarchy system is formed by combining direct connection and centralized switching. The illustration below shows how six telsets are connected using this method.
It is this method that the telephone system is based on.
What method is presently used to connect telephones?
It would be almost impossible to directly connect all the telephones in use today.

Switching is used however, it is not used alone..............
Now, let's see how the hierarchy system of telset connection works for local calls (a local area network).
The local area telephone network starts with individual telsets and an end office.
End offices are connected directly, by two wires, to each telset it services. The end office sends a small amount of current over these wires for telset operation.
Because wires have some resistance to current and the current provided by the end office to the telset is very small, short cable runs connecting small localized areas are used.
The connection between the end office and a telset is called the local loop.
There can be 10,000 local loops for each end office -- numbers 0000 to 9999, the last four digits of telephone numbers.
When an end office runs out of numbers or when a new distant area must be serviced, additional end offices are added to the system.
End offices are identified by using different prefixes, the first three numbers in a telephone number not including the area code.
This allows 1,000 end offices in one local area -- numbers 000 to 999 (10,000 telsets per office for 1,000 offices equals 10 million telsets in one local area!).
End offices are connected by wires, fiber optic cables, or in some instances microwaves. The connections are called interoffice trunks.
When the number of end offices becomes to large, direct connection to each office becomes impractical.
To reduce the number of interoffice trunks and to add flexibility to the network, a tandem (or centralize) switch is added.
The connection to the tandem switch is made using tandem trunks that can be wire cables, fiberoptic cables, or microwave links.
Note that interoffice trunks are still used to connect nearby end offices.
In fact, in some networks, two or more end offices are actually located in the same building and direct connection is the best method.
Also, by using interoffice and tandem trunks, alternate paths exist between end offices that allow switching around equipment failures.
As you have seen, the local area telephone network, hierarchy system, is flexible and can range from one end office to many end offices.
What is the telset directly connected to?
Tandem switches are centralize switches that connect end offices. They do not connect directly to telsets.

The area code is used for long distance identification and is not used to identify telsets in a local area.

Now that you know about your local area network, lets see how a local call is made and some additional functions of an end office.
Your telset is directly connected to an end office using a pair of wires from telephone poles or underground cables.
When you pick up your telset, you make a series circuit that is recognized by the end office as a request for service.
When the user lifts the handset the end office sends the user a dial tone. In the United States the dial tone is continuous tones of 340 and 440 Hz.
The tone informs you that you can "dial in" or "push in" another telsets number.
After you have dialed in or pushed in the number, the end office stores the number and makes the appropriate connection to the called party's local loop.
If the line to the called party is in use or busy, the end office generates a busy signal. In the United States you'll hear a 480 and 620 Hz tone for 0.5 seconds repeated each 0.5 seconds.
If the line is not in use, the end office sends the ring signal to the called party; it varies between countries. The US standard is a 20/30 Hz AC signal at 50/80 volts..
A ring signal is also sent back to you. This lets you know that the party's line is being rung. In the US the return ring is a 2 second tone at 440 and 480 Hz repeating every 4 seconds.
If the called party answers by picking up the telset, another series circuit is made allowing the end office to recognize that the called party answered.
At this time, the connection between the two telsets is made and you can carry on a conversation.
If the called party does not answer, the ring tone will continue until you hang up, breaking your series circuit.
Once your series circuit is broken (no answer or your call is finished) the end office recognizes it and ends the service.

End offices also: send recorded messages, handle different types of services, and determine which path is used when making connections. In direct connections, the telsets are directly connected through the same end office.
In this case, no signal processing (modulation/multiplexing) is used on either end.
Interoffice connections are made when the telsets are directly connected to different end offices and the end offices are connected by interoffice trunks.
In this case, signal processing may be used between end offices but is not used between telsets and end offices.
In tandem switching connections, the telsets are directly connected to different end offices and the end offices are connected by tandem trunks.
In this case, signal processing may be used between end offices and the tandem switch but, is not used between telsets and end offices.
When you pick up a phone, what type of tone indicates that a number can be dialed?
The busy tone tells you that the party you are trying to call is already using their phone. This happens after you have dialed the number.

The ring back tone tells you that the called party you are trying to call is not busy and that their phone is ringing. This happens after the number has been dialed..

Let's now take a closer look at the local loop.............
The end office circuit consists of a center tapped transformer and a talk battery.
In US networks, the talk battery is not a battery but a power supply of either -24 or - 48 volts. Voltages will vary dependent upon the country or local system used.
The secondary side of the transformer forms a balanced circuit that is a two wire loop with both wires being above ground or hot.
When the two wire loop is actuated, DC current flow is not passed to the primary. This is for isolation purposes.
Only AC or pulsating DC signals pass from the secondary to the primary or from the primary to secondary.
Signals that pass from the primary to secondary are the dial tone, busy signal, ring back signal, and incoming voice or recorded message signals.
Signals that pass from the secondary to the primary are out going voice signals and dial signals.
The connection to the telset from the end office is on two wires, tip (green wire) and ring (red wire).
The terms TIP and RING are from the early method of connection using a phone plug.
The green wire connects to the tip terminal of the plug and the red wire connects to the ring terminal.
A third wire may by used to connect the sleeve to a common ground connection.
Today most phone connections use four wires: green, red, yellow, and black.
This allows two separate phone numbers to be used at one location. Special services can also be connected on these extra wires.
In the series circuit, the hook switch, part of the telset, is used to make or break the circuit.
Again, the term "hook switch" is an old term describing how the switch operated on old wall mounted phones that had to be hand cranked.
When the telset is not in use (phone on the hook) the hook switch is open and the series circuit is broken. There is no current flow through the loop.
When the telset is being used (phone off the hook) the hook switch is closed, completing the series circuit and current flows from the end office through the telset back to the end office.
This is the DC current provided by the end office to operate the telset.
The telset also consists of a: dial network, ringer, and voice network.
The ringer circuit is what makes your phone ring and is located before the hook switch.
The signal is AC (20/30 Hz, 50 - 80 volts) and applied to the primary of the transformer. The capacitor blocks DC current.
The dial network is of two types, mechanical (the wheel with holes for each number) and electronic (push button).
The mechanical dialer operates by breaking the circuit path a number of times for each number dialed.
The end office has circuits that count the number of breaks to determine the number dialed.
The electronic dialer operates by pressing buttons that generate different tones.
The end office has circuits that decode the tones to determine the number.
The voice network separates the out going voice signals from the incoming voice signals.
Received voice signals are routed to the output transducer, the speaker.
Transmitted voice signals are routed from the input transducer, microphone, to the loop.
Is the hook switch closed or open when you are using the telset?
When the hook switch is open, no current flows through loop and you can not use the telset.

The ringer circuit rings your telset when someone is calling.

The ringer circuit receives AC power through the transformer.

This completes the information on LOCAL AREA TELEPHONE NETWORK.
1. The hierarchy system is used in the United States to connect telsets by direct connection and centralized switching.
2. Each telset is connected by a local loop to an end office and is identified by the last four digits of a telephone number.
3. End offices are connected by interoffice trunks and are identified by the first three numbers, not including the area code, of telephone numbers.
4. In large area networks, a tandem switch is used........
5. A call is made by you picking up the telset and making a series circuit giving you a dial tone.
6. The end office then stores the dialed number and makes the proper connection.
7. Busy, ring, ring back, recorded messages, and other services are performed by the end office.
8. The local loop consists of a center tapped transformer, talk battery, two wire loop, and the telset.
9. The telset consists of a ringer circuit, hook switch, dialer network, and voice network.

LONG DISTANCE PHONE NETWORKWORK
The local area network is only part of a telephone system..
DISCUSSION
To complete a telephone system, long distance calling must be made available.
You should know that by dialing a 1 before a 7 digit telephone number, you can make long distance calls in your general area.
Or by dialing a 1 before a 10 digit telephone number (3 digit area code plus 7 digit number), you can make long distance calls to almost anywhere in the world.
A typical system that allows long distance calls uses additional offices.
Your telset, local loop, and end office network remains the same.
Recall that even though you can choose different telephone companies, you do not have to change telsets or add more wires to your house.
Your local loop always remains the same.
The difference is that when you dial a "1", the end office routes your call to a toll office - long distance costs you additional money!
The toll office is where the switching to other offices is determined and the billing information is stored.
From the toll office, your call is routed to various intermediate switching offices.
The number, location, and name of the intermediate switching offices depends on where your long distance call is going.
Then, your call is routed back to a toll office in the area you are calling.
And finally to the called party's end office and telset.

Which office stores long distance billing information?
The end office switches your call to a toll office for long distance calling. The end office does not store billing information.

The signal processing methods used in a long distance telephone network vary.
Remember, between the telset and end office, no signal processing methods are used.
But, signal processing may be used, and is normally used, between the other offices.
The most common methods of signal processing used by end offices, toll offices, and intermediate switching offices is modulation and multiplexing.
Modulation is used when the connection between the offices use microwaves or fiberoptic cable as the transmission medium.
Note that if a call is modulated for transmitting through the air, it can still be multiplexed.
And, if a call is modulated/multiplexed on the sending side, it must be demodulated/demultiplexed on the receiving side.
In a long distance telephone network, where is signal processing not used?
Connections from end offices to toll offices normally use at least one method of signal processing.
TRY AGAIN!
Connections from toll offices to end offices normally use at least one method of signal processing.
TRY AGAIN!
Which method of signal processing reduces the number of fiberoptic cables needed to route calls?
Amplification is normally used throughout a long distance network to compensate for attenuation. Amplification does not reduce the hardware required to transmit calls......
TRY AGAIN!
Modulation is a method that allows signals to be sent through the air. Modulation does not reduce the hardware required to transmit calls.

This network is generic and is used to illustrate a long distance telephone network.
The network has five levels of hierarchy...................
Class 5 is the local area telephone network.
The second level of hierarchy is class 4 which are toll offices. There are less toll offices than local area networks.
Classes 3, 2, and 1 make up the intermediate switching offices. Class 3 offices are called primary offices.
Note that there are less class 3 offices than class 4 and, how the offices are cross connected.
Class 2 offices are called sectional offices.
Again, note that there are less class 2 offices and how cross connections are used.
Class 1 offices are called regional offices.
Again notice that class 1 has less offices than class 2 and cross connection is used.
The advantage of cross connection is that calls can be routed around failed equipment and busy circuits.
The advantage of using less offices is that calls do not have to go through the entire system.
A long distance call may only use class 5 and 4 offices.
Or, only class 5, 4, and 3 offices. It all depends on the distance of the call.
